extraction.name: OpenBookQA
extraction.description: OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset modeled after open book exams. It consists of about 6000 4-way multiple-choice questions paired with a set of 1326 elementary level science facts. Answering questions requires combining an open book fact with broad common knowledge, probing multi-hop reasoning.
extraction.creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Heidelberg University)
extraction.citeAs: Mihaylov et al. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. arXiv:1809.02789.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated via a multi-stage crowdsourcing and partial expert filtering process. Crowd-workers were shown a science fact, asked to think of a second common fact, then convert a derived assertion into a 4-way multiple-choice question. Questions were filtered for hardness (IR and word-association solvers must fail), answerability (at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers must answer correctly), and answer choice de-biasing. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web API, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Overall, 8140 questions were collected, of which 2183 were discarded in crowdsourcing Step 7 (answerability check).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The open book F is a subset of the WorldTree corpus, specifically the 2287 WorldTree facts marked as 'central' by the original authors in at least one explanation, further filtered to 1326 facts that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered using: (1) basic checks (exactly 4 answer choices, no negation words, uniform answer choice length); (2) automatic hardness filter requiring both an IR solver and a word-association solver to fail; (3) crowd answerability filter requiring at least 4 out of 5 workers to answer correctly; (4) random shuffling of answer choices to remove position bias; (5) expert review for Dev and Test splits.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers were shown a science fact f, asked to think of a second common fact k, derive a new assertion, convert it into a 4-way multiple-choice question, and verify it is hard for IR and word-association solvers. Five additional workers then answered each question to verify answerability. The question author also provided an interpretation of the additional fact k needed. Dev and Test sets were further reviewed by an in-house expert.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was estimated using a statistical model based on Hoeffding's Inequality applied to the 5 crowd-worker answers per question. The estimate H(Q) >= H_tilde(Q) - 3% holds with probability over 98.8%. Additionally, 5 new annotations were obtained for 100 randomly chosen questions from each split to validate the estimate.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Human bias in crowdsourced answer choices was identified: workers tend to start with the correct answer and then create three incorrect ones that are often homogeneous or share common properties uncharacteristic of the correct answer. Additionally, 'Choice A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions before shuffling. A 'plausible answer detector' ignoring the question achieved 49.6% accuracy, and an 'odd-one-out solver' achieved 50.2%, highlighting these biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The additional facts K provided by crowd-workers were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question, and should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts or a substitute for broad common knowledge. In 21% of analyzed training questions, the crowdsourced question actually tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development (validation), and testing of question answering systems that require multi-hop reasoning combining provided science facts with broad common knowledge. The dataset includes the core fact f as intermediate supervision for Train and Dev questions.

name.evidence: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject.

description.evidence: The OpenBookQA dataset consists of about 6,000 4-way multiple-choice questions, each associated with one core fact from a 'book' F of 1326 such facts, and an auxiliary set K of about 6000 additional facts.

url.evidence: The dataset and the code for the models are available at http://data.allenai.org/OpenBookQA .

creator.evidence: Todor Mihaylov and Peter Clark and Tushar Khot and Ashish Sabharwal, Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Seattle, WA, U.S.A.; Research Training Group AIPHES & Heidelberg University, Heidelberg, Germany

publisher.evidence: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Seattle, WA, U.S.A.

inLanguage.evidence: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We used a multi-stage process starting with F, using crowd-sourcing to generate (noisy) questions based on F that probe novel situations, using an automatic filter to ensure hardness for retrieval and association based systems, using a crowd filter to ensure answerability by a lay person, and further using an expert filter to ensure higher quality in Dev and Test sets.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification. ... The Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert to ensure higher quality.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Overall, 8140 questions were collected, of which 2183 were discarded in crowdsourcing Step 7.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: For F, we use a subset of the WorldTree corpus which Jansen et al. (2018) have analyzed for sufficiency for elementary level science. The subset we use is taken from the 2287 WorldTree facts that were marked as 'central' by the original authors in at least one explanation. We further filter them down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The system verifies qmc passes basic checks such as uniformity of answer choices... w then feeds the multiple-choice question qmc to an information retrieval solver and a word association based solver, and verifies that (a) neither of them answers qmc correctly... Question qmc is then shown to 5 new crowd-workers, who are asked to answer it. If at least 4 out of 5 workers answer qmc correctly, it is deemed answerable... The answer choices of qmc are randomly shuffled to avoid unintended bias. The Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert to ensure higher quality.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: A crowd-worker w is shown a random science fact f from the set F. w is asked to think of a second common fact, k, that may be combined with f to derive a new, valid assertion s. w then converts s into a question-answer pair and extends this into a 4-way multiple choice question by adding 3 incorrect answer choices... The Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert to ensure higher quality.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: An application of Hoeffding's Inequality shows that H_tilde(Q) converges to H(Q) very rapidly... In our Dev and Test sets, where |Q|=500 and |I|=5, this translates into H(Q) being at least H_tilde(Q) - 3% with probability over 98.8%... we also obtained 5 new annotations for 100 randomly chosen questions from each of Train, Dev, and Test sets. The performance remained similar at 88.6%, 90.2%, and 91.6%, resp.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: Question qmc is then shown to 5 new crowd-workers, who are asked to answer it.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Motivated by recent findings of gameability of NLP datasets (Gururangan et al., 2018), we also develop and evaluate simple, attention-based, neural baselines including a plausible answer detector (which ignores the question text completely) and an odd-one-out solver. These highlight inevitable human bias in any crowdsourced dataset... Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of the questions at the end of Step 4.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: These second facts, unfortunately, were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to q. We thus include in OpenBookQA the set K of such second facts only as auxiliary data for optional use. We emphasize that K should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts, or as a substitute for broad common knowledge.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: To encourage further research on this new task, for each Train and Dev question q, OpenBookQA also includes f as intermediate supervision signal, which may be viewed as a partial explanation for q. We leave closing the large gap to human performance as a challenge for the NLP community.
